blocks.text: Pass a request along a chain of handlers, where each one either handles it or forwards it to the next.

The sender knows only the first link. Each **handler** inspects the request and chooses: answer it and **stop**, change it and **forward**, or do both around the rest of the chain. The chain's order is the policy, and handlers can be added, removed or reordered without touching the sender or each other.

items: **Varies:** which handlers exist and their order.
**Stays stable:** the sender and the request type.
**Short-circuit:** any handler may end the chain early.

blocks.text: Middleware pipelines (servlet filters, Netty, OkHttp interceptors) are the dominant modern form: every link runs, and each decides whether to continue.

walkthrough.note: `Filter` receives the request and a `Next` representing the rest of the chain. Calling `next.proceed` is the only way forward, so every filter controls continuation.
The chain is built from the end: each filter is bound to the already-built remainder. The result is a single `Next` the caller can invoke.
`auth` stops the chain with 401 when there is no user. `limit` counts requests per user and stops with 429 after two. Otherwise both forward.
The terminal handler does the real work. Order is explicit: authentication runs before rate limiting, so anonymous callers are never counted.
The anonymous request stops at `auth`. The third request from `ann` is stopped by `limit`; the application handler never runs for either.

blocks.text: Fraud screening before a card payment is authorized.

A payment passes through a blocklist check, a velocity check, a geo-mismatch check and an amount threshold, in that order. Each rule can approve, reject, or defer to the next one. Cheap checks come first so most transactions leave early, and risk teams reorder or add rules from configuration, with no change to the payment service.

blocks.text: Payoff: rules are independent and individually testable, and their order and membership are configuration, not code.

lists.title: Use when
items: Several objects may handle a request and the right one is not known up front.
Processing steps should be added, removed or reordered by configuration.
Cross-cutting checks (auth, limits, logging) wrap a core handler.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Exactly one handler is known from the request: pick it directly.
Every step must run regardless; a plain list loop is simpler.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: A request that falls off the end unhandled needs an explicit terminal.
Order bugs: a limiter before auth counts anonymous traffic.
Hard-to-debug flow; log which link decided.
A handler that forgets to forward silently ends the chain.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A chain with two links that never change.
Handlers sharing mutable request state in hidden ways.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: A functional interface plus a fold over a list builds the chain without handler base classes.
A sealed result type makes handled, rejected and passed outcomes explicit.

rows.difference: Both wrap a successor behind one interface. A decorator always delegates and adds behavior; a chain handler may stop and answer the request itself.
Observer notifies every subscriber and none can veto the others. A chain stops at the first handler that claims the request.
Strategy picks one algorithm up front. A chain lets each handler decide at runtime whether the request is its.
Requests in a chain are often command objects, so a handler can queue, log or reject them.
A composite fans an operation out to all children and combines results. A chain passes one request along a line until it is handled.

entries.detail: Each `Filter` calls `chain.doFilter(request, response)` to continue or returns early to short-circuit.

entries.name: ChannelPipeline
entries.detail: An ordered list of `ChannelHandler`s; each uses `ctx.fireChannelRead` to pass an event to the next.

entries.name: SecurityFilterChain
entries.detail: An ordered list of security filters, with `FilterChainProxy` selecting the chain that matches the request.

exercises.prompt: Explain Chain of Responsibility in your own words: who decides where a request stops, and how does it differ from Decorator?

modelAnswer.text: A request enters the first handler of an ordered chain. Each handler decides: handle it and stop, or forward it to the next, possibly after changing it. The sender knows only the head, so handlers can be added or reordered freely. A decorator also wraps a successor but always delegates; a chain handler can end the request.

keyPoints: Sender knows only the first link
Each handler decides to handle, forward, or both
Order is the policy and is configurable
A handler can short-circuit; a decorator always delegates
Needs a terminal for unhandled requests
